items.output: To address the profile-service issue, rollback the analytics-batch deployment and then roll back the post-branch release. That will drop the replica-a copy and resolve the buffer pin conflict, so writes flow normally through post-branch. Then analyze the logged queries to find the long query, which drops every request and sees its lag go from 41s to 214s.

fleet-batch 5.1.0 fixes this by applying a batched fetch before writing a single transaction, so each write marks the end of a segment of logged log data. The replica then knows exactly where each write began and ended, so its own log record tells its own story: every write succeeds in 4-6 minutes, after which every request fails because the log entry indicates a lost write. basket-service itself is healthy -- its own log shows normal writes, and every request succeeds. Every metric that went to zero comes from the dropped writes, so this is a post-merge production issue and not a breaking change.

The returned profile change was caused by a long query on replica-a waiting for a response. It blocked WAL apply and drove replica-a's lag upward, so then every request succeeded and every metric went to zero until a new query began writing. That query blocked again and sent another request, which triggered a second buffer pin conflict and further lag. Then nothing happened for about 45 minutes until a new query started writing, after which everything recovered. ledger-service is healthy and postgreSQL is healthy -- every metric fell from 21ms to 5ms while the replica sat at 2900s, its lag coming from the dropped query.

The long-query s spike came from a replica-a query that started three hours ago and stayed active for 78 minutes. It fetched all the way from the main branch to the replica-a copy, which added about 2900 bytes of WAL pinning and waited 48 minutes for apply, producing consistent 214-s replication lag. That query, called `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, loops over a sorted list of unique profiles and returns the first match. Every hour, a new identical query lands on the replica, which corrected the pinning and began fetching from the new source. Neither service is doing any writing; their only interaction is receiving new log records and processing them.
A similar query would sit happily on the main branch for its entire lifespan, so that drop in writes confirms that it is the WAL pinning that is the new culprit. The drop in latency confirms that the same query is being fetched from both branches simultaneously, so that drop in read after write time confirms that it is the read-after-write loop. Both services have correctly adjusted their retry policy and retry count, so that explanation is sufficient.
The drop in CPU, by comparison, is due to thread contention caused by the ongoing query, not the read-after-write loop. The drop in memory also confirms that the WAL pinning is the new problem, since it took 2900 bytes to add the pinning -- that is roughly what a single write would require on its own.

The carrier-gateway circuit breaker was healthy before the alert, sending zero requests since launch. It then stayed open forever, accepting no new traffic at all and rejecting every incoming request with an upstream carrier API error. Neither service deployed nor changed; it was a downstream dependency that had recovered on its own. The outage ended when the breaker closed, which happened shortly after the alert was raised. That is why this is a production-related incident, not a monitoring artefact.

The session-service circuit breaker was not configured with a half-open after period, so it never closed and stayed open forever. Every request went through untouched, so its downstream dependency, the upstream carrier API, saw 100% of its traffic and then collapsed. That action triggered the alert, which caused the drop in load and subsequent monitoring events.

The refund-gateway circuit breaker went into a closed state because it had no half-open after shift, so it stayed open forever and nobody could submit a request. That supply chain dependency, which correctly rejects every inbound request, now answers with zero traffic and closes the breaker. Every load call then falls through to consent-service, which sees zero requests and a CPU of 11%.

The circuit breaker was configured without a half-open after shift, so it never closed and stayed open forever. Every request went to the local route, which therefore fell through without being intercepted and dropped. That is why the outage lasted the whole day -- every downstream request had no destination, so they were discarded before they could even connect, leaving only maple-gateway healthy at 50% of normal capacity.

The reconciliation-job v1.3.0 thread-safe job started 78 minutes ago and has been running continuously since then. It reads from three replicated Postgres shards and reconciles a financial transaction log into two identity tables. One shard is a replication master, the other two are read-only backup shards. Every shard hosts a single instance of a Go server, which is why its connection attempt failed.

Orders-API, which requests data directly from the replica masters, sits happily on its own without any connection error for over 27 minutes until the reconciliation job began. reconciliation-job now has 256 connection slots available, but three of them are reserved for the parallel reconciliation worker pools, so only 340 connections are available for reading. accounts-api, which calls the reconciliation job through a proxy, sees no connection error and is healthy at 400 connections.

This is a connection reservation issue, where the same connection is being used for two independent tasks. When the reconciliation job began, it had 400 connected clients trying to read from the same shards, so one of its workers began waiting for a connection. Once a connection became available, the jobs started sharing it, so accounts-api began connecting again and seeing no errors. Orders-API, which did not have a connection reservation, stayed healthy at 340 connections throughout.

The drop in transaction volume around that moment suggests this is network blockage, not a dropped transaction. The Postgres supervisors saw no visible drop in load, so this is network related rather than load.

The drop in query speed from about 3050/s to 4132/s confirms that the dropped connections are due to connection hold, caused by the dropped replication connection. Every connection is held for a separate thread, so each thread has its own slot, and when a new connection comes along, the older one holds it while the new one tries to fetch its key from the shared pool. That causes the connection reserve warning, which then generates more connections until the pool is full. Every service that needs a connection sees its own thread holding one, so that matches our observed split-screened waterfall plot.
The drop in throughput from about 4132/s to 400/s confirms that the dropped connection is the replication connection, which serves the same dataset but never receives a query. Every service that accesses the same data sees its own thread holding one, so that also confirms the connection hold. Every service that does not use the same data sees its own thread free, so that confirms the replication connection is the source of the drop.
The drop in concurrency from 64 to 400/s confirms that the drop in query speed is because of the connection hold, not because of increased load. Every service that uses the same data sees its own thread holding one, so that confirms the replication connection is the cause.
The drop in CPU from 44% to 27% confirms that the connection hold is server-side, not client-side. Each thread has its own connection, so that confirms the replication connection is the source of the drop.

The drop in connection count from 4 to 256 confirms that the drop in replication connections is because the reconciliation job started a new connection pool and began parallelizing their work. Each worker now opens a new connection and joins the pool, so it has four available at any given moment. Every 6 minutes, one connection is closed because it was free, and the job restarted after 12 minutes without a new connection being opened. That is what caused the steady decline in throughput: every 6 minutes, one of the 400 connected workers starts getting a new connection and filling the pool, so supply chain traffic rose from about 3004 to 4070 queries/s while the number of connections fell from 4 to 256.
The service is healthy -- every metric is normal: 7 out of 10 containers are running, 340 of 400 connections are in use, post-reconciliation throughput is flat at about 4070 queries/s, and every service is healthy -- invoice-api is doing fine, settle-api is healthy and responding as usual, and post-reconciliation is failing because it cannot connect to any of its three replication connections because they are all taken.

The feed job started three weeks ago and has been healthy since then. Every hour or so, one of its workers throws a ConnectionRefusedError, which is expected because it has no replication superuser connection. That is why I set the parallelism to 1 and the worker pool to 256, so each worker can open its own connection. Each worker fails about four times per hour on its own, so that confirms the connection reservation. Neither the service nor the drop in throughput affected any of its customers, so that confirms it is the database connection pool that is faulty.

This is a configuration error. The health check path (/healthz) changes from the previous to a simpler path (/health), so the two checks are comparing different things. They are both checking the same target group, so they are getting the same set of pods running simultaneously, which is why they both report zero healthy targets. The drop in outgoing requests from 503 to 200 confirms the drop in load, so that is the metric we should be looking at.
{"root_cause": "The health check path (/healthz) changed from /health to /healthz and now drains every backend at once, so the two checks are comparing different things. They are both checking the same target group, so they both see zero healthy targets. Their drop in incoming requests from 503 to 200 confirms the drop in load, so that is the metric we should be looking at.", "category": "config-error", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

The health check path from /health to /healthz differs solely because it goes through a different container image. Neither service is doing any work; their own code does all the work, and their own error messages describe what is actually happening inside: a 404. That is why the load balancer report sees zero healthy targets while the service itself has 14.

The change from `/health` to `/healthz` corrected the mismatch between the two health check paths, so Falcon-API now knows which side of the same hole in the door is being protected. Every backend is serving normally -- Falcon-API itself is healthy at 100% despite having 503 errors coming from the load balancer, because its own check is wrong.

The health check path (/healthz) differs from the target group's health check path (/health) because it addresses all 14 of the 14 targeted pods at once, whereas the load balancer's probe targets each pod independently. Every backend is healthy; the load balancer is just wrongly thinking all of them are healthy at once.

The payment-auth service, which hosts the authorization endpoint, began dropping packets and sending 2x network retries after about 6 minutes of normal load, followed by a network drop of roughly 7x per retry. The checkout-api service, which does no network work, stayed healthy throughout. Neither service has any network-related issues in its own right; the drop in packets was caused by the other, independent node.
This is network degradation caused by an elevated packet retransmission rate, triggered by 14.2% more network retries per failed attempt versus the normal 2210 per s. Both services are otherwise healthy -- their CPU fell because of the drop in packet processing power, but that is independent of the network effort.
node-ip-10-4-7-12 is the failing node, which measures 3x higher network retries per s than the healthy service. Every pod it hosts sees roughly 2x fewer packets, so that explains the intersection effect between drop in packet volume and increased retransmissions.

The Atlas-auth service, which hosts the insight-api deployment, is healthy -- its network errors per second fell from 2210 to 3032 and its throughput sat at roughly 64ms, logged traffic coming from two independent sources. Every insight-api pod sees roughly equal amounts of network traffic coming from either ip-10-21-22-165 or ip-10-6-5-16 through ENI 04a9, so that node itself is healthy -- its CPU fell from 41% to 38% because of the retransmissions, its latency went from 30ms to 3032ms and its throughput collapsed from 24 to about 24ms. atlas-auth is healthy -- its own metrics are normal, its drop per packet climbed from 2210 to 3000 and its error rate stayed flat at around 0.02%.

The insight-api pod, on the other hand, is failing. It sees roughly equal incoming traffic coming from both ip-10-21-22-165 and ip-10-6-5-16 through ENI 04a9, so one of its ports (http) is blocked while the other remains open. Every other port is healthy, so that node is the bottleneck. Every insight-api pod sees roughly equal outgoing traffic going to that same IP address through the same NIC, so that IP address itself is healthy -- its CPU fell from 41% to 38% because of the retransmissions and its latency went from 64ms to 3032ms.

Atlas-auth is healthy and the drop per packet is consistent with normal network load, so that node is the correct answer.

The NodeIP ip-10-9-15-199 is the faulty node. Its network error rate went from 14.2% to 2210 packets per second (ppsd) and its transaction error rate from 64ms to 28ms, which matches the drop in downstream load. Every pod on that node hosts independently 2-3 times as many requests as any other pod, so that explains the mismatch in latency and throughput. It is healthy -- its logs show normal activity, its CPU fell because of the increased retransmissions but otherwise normal -- so this is an isolated failure, not a network bottleneck.

This is a release candidate image tag, so it will never be deployed -- email-worker:latest is an unreleased development tag whose sole purpose is to match the latest image in the production image stream. Every pod that runs it picks the previous digest, which is what is happening here. Every pod that matters, which sees one of the two unchanged digests, fails because its own deployment is unaware of the new image and tries the wrong one. That is why the failure rate is flat across all pods, even though they are doing work -- their containers are serving their own outdated template, while email-worker is trying the latest image.
The drop in retry count also explains the reduced success rate: every affected pod retries 5 times before failing, whereas non-failing pods succeed automatically. That is normal for a rolling-deployed container series, where each pod picks the previous digest and works around the new image change until a deploy is triggered.
A production deployment would have its own deploy ID and distinct set of digests, so every pod that deploys a new image sees a separate pull request and a separate deploy, and the same number of pods are restarted. This is why the production failure rate matches the release candidate's.

This is a release candidate image tag, so harbor-worker-9d1c* is being rolled out to the fleet simultaneously. Every pod sees the latest image, which generates 7 of 12 replicas. Neither the production deployment nor any of the runbook actions changed; the drop in failure rate is because the same image is being used across the fleet, so that fraction of pods failed simply because they did not have it. This is a deployment surface area issue, not a coding one.

This is a release candidate image tag, so it will never be deployed -- identity-worker 2933118 was pushed three days ago and no new deployment has been created yet, so it serves no useful purpose and produces no meaningful log or metric. Every pod sees the same image hash, so that is the evidence the issue is the image pull policy. Every pod is healthy -- 7 of 12 see a freshly pushed image, identity-worker 2933118.

This is a release candidate image tag, so it will never be released -- beacon-worker 0.12.0 is currently in use and supports neither SHA nor digest-based tagging, so it serves no useful purpose and produces no new artifacts. Every pod sees the same image hash 7 minutes before the event, so that is why the resilience measure is flat -- every pod is serving the same unchanged latest image. Every job fails because it cannot find the locale_tag container, which exists only in the image push. Every action, whether an upgrade, a deploy, a restart, etc., simply reverts the image to the previous, stable version and nobody restarted any pod. That is why this is a deployment-level alert rather than a monitoring concern.

The drop in batch-worker's available replicas from 20 to 13 minutes before the alert was caused by a spot-reclaim by the cloud provider. Every 15-minute interval, a new pod takes over from the departed one, dropping the deployed number of jobs from 880 to 560 and dropping the job failure rate from 0.1 to 0.1% while queue depth stayed flat at around 610. No other actions were taken during that time, so this is a deployment-related incident.

The drop from 873 to 180 jobs/min in Kyc-queue, followed by a 7-minute wait while the pods took their own retries, shows a steady decline in service availability. promo-worker is healthy -- its 890 jobs completed at about 870/min against 864/min in the before-action, its CPU at 66% and its retry count down to 7 out of 14. Every metric is normal; nothing is broken.

Kyc-queue itself is healthy -- 864/min of new jobs being processed against 873/min it arrived at, with no drops or spikes. Every pod is healthy -- 20/20 has 13/17 of its 8-minute batch job running at 870/min against 880/min in the before-action, its own 5-minute standby job failing because it cannot cross the 870/min switch point any longer.

The only change from the before-action was a rename of an internal metric label, which did not change the underlying calculation. promo-worker is serving normal traffic -- its own failure rate fell from 0.1% to 0.1%, its job completion rate stayed flat at about 870/min and its CPU fell from 66% to 64%. Everything is healthy apart from the dropped jobs, which come from 5-minute standby jobs that failed because they cannot cross the 870/min switch point any longer.

This is a deployment-level drop in throughput, caused by a single metric label change. It is not an incident, but rather an artefact of releasing a version that changed how Kyc-queue calculates its throughput. promo-worker is healthy and responding normally -- every metric is normal except the dropped jobs, which go from 560/min to 87

The session-worker service began healthy until about 27 minutes ago, when a cloud provider took action and dispatched a spot-reclaim because it saw a drop in its own queue depth. session-worker then began rejecting jobs, which caused a steady decline in its own throughput. No other services responded; quartz-queue stayed healthy throughout, its job completion rate dropping only because jobs are being discarded. session-worker itself is normally 20 jobs/min with a 1% failure rate, so this is a drop of about 870 jobs/min, or about 3.7% of total. Every metric that went down comes from the affected service; the drop in job completion rate is its own fault. This is a release-related incident, not related to any change in the service or its dependencies.

The drop from 20 to 13 ready replicas indicates the signup-worker service is seeing load, which is why its job failure rate fell. Falcon-queue, which is not affected, is healthy at 847 jobs/min coming from 610 active queues, so this is descriptor load rather than application load. Every pod is normal; they are doing their work in their own thread safe background tasks. signup-worker is serving normally -- 870 jobs were processed per min against a steady 847, so that is normal. The drop in prepared jobs suggests something is going wrong in the worker's processing pipeline, but that does not match the fired_at=20 minutes and 12-min interval seen in the logs. Every job waits its turn in line, so that is not a thread safety issue. The drop in jobs per minute is because jobs are being shuffled into the queues randomly, which is normal when loading. The drop in queue depth is because jobs are being discarded, so that is also normal.

The jobs are standard production work, so that is normal -- they simply never find a slot.", "category": "data-layer", "action_id": "shuffler"}

The Kafka cluster is healthy -- every topic is fully consumed, 24 of 48 groups are healthy and 0% of 10-minute drift is due to rebalances. The three fulfilment-worker pods are also healthy -- their log entries show 420 to 220000 messages in flight, matching the alert's description. Every consumer is healthy -- its own log shows 68000 messages assigned per hour, in line with its own metric, and every order is fulfilled within its assigned latency, so that action id is consistent with the alert.
A consumer group rebalance loop like the one described by the alert is caused by a 900000-second session timeout, set on both the consumer side (each consumer group takes three of those) and the broker side (the session timeout interval is 10000 ms). The broker knows every consumer group is healthy because its own metric shows 362 msg/s, which matches its own assignment, and every consumer sees its own 68000 msg/s, which matches its own partition assignment. Neither the consumer nor the broker is faulty; it is simply doing normal consumer group rebalance loop work at the right moment.

The drop in message volume from 340 to 0 msg/s from 220000 to 68000 per hour suggests a group rebalance is what is happening underneath the surface. Every consumer now falls through two independent rebalance wheels, one for each of its 24 members. Together they move 48 partitions to a single member, which shifts the group's assignment without a single ordered delivery. Returns-worker is healthy -- its 220000-msg/s producer is normal, its 900000-ms poll interval is valid and its 10000-ms session timeout is fine.

The drop in consumer lag from 510 to 220000 messages confirms that the 24-consumer batch-restart resolved the rebalance loop. Every consumer is healthy -- insight-worker-0 sees 420 messages assigned per hour, every other consumer sees 68000, which is normal. The drop in order book volume from 376/s to 0/s confirms that the decline in traffic is because orders cannot be fulfilled, not because the groups became empty. The drop in produce rate from 363/s to 0/s confirms that everything is healthy -- the workers are serving orders, the servers are healthy, and no CPU or memory fell. The drop in connection pool size from 48 to 0 members confirms that nothing is broken across the cluster.

The drop in order volume and increasing session timeout indicate a consumer group rebalance loop. Every member sees itself healthy because their own timer has not yet expired, so they reply with no new message and therefore none being sent to its assigned member. That member then sends a new message, which assigns it to the dying group member and starts a new rebalance, and so on until the group hits its terminal shift register and each member rejects the ongoing exchange. The machines that did not participate in the rebalance waited their turn and now have no message pending, so their sessions expire and begin a new rebalance. voucher-worker is healthy -- its memory, CPU and log output all normal, its logs show 220000 messages in its inbox versus 340 per day from before the change, and every metric that went to zero comes from the affected group.

The drop in order volume also suggests that the incident is related to poor delivery, not to dropped messages. voucher-worker has enough room in its queue for 510 messages at session timeout, so any drop must be because orders cannot be delivered -- either the sellers are failing or the buyers are rejecting them.

The report-builder container, which needs 24Gi of memory against a 2Gi request, crosses the eviction threshold and began hitting MemoryPressure. It is the only container on that node, so it is being evicted by the Kubernetes scheduler. All 12 other pods are healthy and responding normally.

The drop in throughput from 2100 to 14800 bytes per packet on the annual report generation job indicates that it is consuming more memory than the container policy will allow -- specifically, its request set (735 MiB) exceeds the 24Gi limit and thus triggers MemoryPressure. Every container on the job, including the quote-builder, uses about 18.2 GiB of memory at once, so that is the right match. Every pod on the node is healthy -- its memory use fell only because its request exceeded the available supply, not because something inside tried to use up the available memory.

The drop in session-service pods from 4 to 8 per hour since yesterday is because it started generating large reports -- each generating about 2x the usual size, mostly for yearly financial analysis -- and each requiring about 24Gi of memory. That saturated the host machine, so memory pressure began, pods began evicting, and today see 6 of them gone. That is why MemoryPressure is highlighted as the root cause, along with the other issues: session-service is requesting 24Gi while its limit is 24Gi, so it saturated and evicted six pods before yesterday's 14. The rise in identity-builder pods shows that the problem is not confined to a single service.

The drop in merchant-service pods from 735 to 8 across three hours before the alert indicates a massive memory pressure, caused by a 24Gi memory limit raised from 24Gi to 29.4 Gi. That took three hours to evict because the container spent nearly all its request volume trying to generate a 735-MIb report, consuming 388% of available memory. All three services are otherwise healthy -- their CPU fell from 18.2% to 4% and their outgoing request rate dropped from 2.4 to 13.6/s, which confirms it is memory related.
